summary.text: A refracting telescope is an optical telescope that uses a lens as its objective to form an image.
It typically has a lens at the front, then a long tube, then an eyepiece or instrumentation at the rear where the view comes to focus.
Refractors were the earliest type of optical telescope, but for most research they have been replaced by reflectors, which allow larger apertures.

facts.label: Magnification rule
facts.value: Objective focal length divided by eyepiece focal length

facts.label: First record
facts.value: Netherlands, about 1608, in an unsuccessful patent attempt

facts.label: Galileo's strongest
facts.value: 980 millimeters long, magnifying objects about 30 times

facts.label: Achromatic lens
facts.value: Invented in 1733 by Chester Moore Hall

items.prompt: You keep the same front lens on a refractor but swap in an eyepiece with a shorter focal length. What happens to the magnification?

options.label: It stays the same, since the front lens alone sets it
It goes up, because the eyepiece's focal length is the divisor
It goes down, because a stronger eyepiece spreads the light
It drops to zero until the tube is shortened

items.explain: Magnification is the objective's focal length divided by the eyepiece's, so a shorter eyepiece focal length gives a bigger result.

items.prompt: A stargazer swaps a concave eyepiece for a convex one in a simple lens telescope. What is the trade?

options.label: A narrower view but an upright image
A sharper image with the same field of view
A shorter tube but a dimmer image
A wider view and more eye relief, but an inverted image

items.explain: A convex eyepiece makes the emerging rays converge, which allows a much wider field of view and greater eye relief, but the image is inverted.

items.prompt: Galileo covered part of his front lens with a stop that shrank it. Why?

options.label: Lens quality was poor, and a smaller opening limited image flaws
He wanted a brighter picture of the Moon
The tube was too short to hold a wider lens
Larger lenses could not be bought in Venice

items.explain: With the poor lens technology of the time, he used aperture stops to cut the lens diameter and limit aberrations, at the cost of a blurry view with a narrow field.

items.prompt: Early refractors needed enormous focal lengths to keep their flaws down. What design change let later ones be shorter?

options.label: A much larger single-piece glass lens at the front
A longer tube holding a stronger eyepiece
A front lens made of two glass pieces with different dispersion
A thin silver coating added to the front lens

items.explain: Single-element lenses needed very high focal ratios. The achromatic lens combined crown and flint glass to reduce aberrations and allowed shorter focal lengths.

items.prompt: Big refractors were popular in the late 1800s. Why do most research telescopes now take another approach?

options.label: Refractors cannot magnify anything
Mirror-based designs allow larger apertures
Refractors were banned from observatories
Mirror-based designs are always shorter

items.explain: For most research purposes, the refractor has been superseded by the reflecting telescope, which allows larger apertures.

items.prompt: You watch a bird through Galileo's style of telescope, which has no intermediary focus. How does the bird appear?

options.label: Upside down, as in all telescopes
Mirrored left to right
Blurred beyond recognition
The right way up

items.explain: Because the Galilean design has no intermediary focus, the image is non-inverted, meaning upright.
